one_liner_plain: Injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks prevented HIV in women better than daily oral PrEP

citation.title: Cabotegravir for the prevention of HIV-1 in women: results from HPTN 084, a phase 3, randomised clinical trial
citation.authors: Delany-Moretlwe S, Hughes JP, Bock P, et al.

sections.background: Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) works when it is taken, and it has been introduced in more than 70 countries. But women face real barriers to a daily pill, including stigma, judgement, and the fear of violence, and in sub-Saharan Africa women and girls account for most new HIV infections. Long-acting cabotegravir, an integrase inhibitor given as an intramuscular injection every 8 weeks, had already outperformed oral PrEP in men and transgender women in HPTN 083. HPTN 084 asked the same question in cisgender women.

methods.design: Phase 3, randomized (1:1), double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled superiority trial at 20 clinical research sites in seven countries in sub-Saharan Africa.
methods.population: HIV-negative people assigned female at birth, aged 18-45 years, at risk of HIV, reporting at least two episodes of vaginal intercourse in the previous 30 days, and using long-acting reversible contraception. {{n:n_total}} were enrolled ({{n:n_cab}} cabotegravir, {{n:n_tdf}} TDF-FTC).
methods.intervention: Cabotegravir 600 mg intramuscular injection at weeks 5 and 9 and every 8 weeks thereafter (after a 5-week oral lead-in), plus daily oral TDF-FTC placebo.
methods.comparator: Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus emtricitabine (TDF-FTC) plus placebo injections.
methods.primary_endpoint: Incident HIV infection (intention-to-treat); safety: grade 2 or higher clinical and laboratory adverse events.
methods.follow-up: Median 1.2 years in the blinded phase, which was stopped early after the efficacy result.

sections.results: There were {{n:inf_total}} incident HIV infections over 3898 person-years: {{n:inf_cab}} in the cabotegravir group ({{n:inc_cab}} per 100 person-years) and {{n:inf_tdf}} in the TDF-FTC group ({{n:inc_tdf}} per 100 person-years). The hazard ratio was {{n:hr}} (95% CI 0.05 to 0.31; p<0.0001), with a risk difference of {{n:rd}}. Why the gap? Adherence. In a random subset of TDF-FTC participants, only {{n:adh}} of plasma samples showed tenofovir levels consistent with daily use, whereas injection coverage was {{n:cov}} of person-years. Adverse events were similar between groups except injection-site reactions, which were more common with cabotegravir ({{n:isr_cab}} vs {{n:isr_tdf}}) but did not lead anyone to stop injections. Confirmed pregnancy incidence was 1.3 per 100 person-years, with no congenital anomalies reported.
sections.conclusions: Both products were generally safe, well tolerated, and effective, but injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks was superior to daily oral TDF-FTC in preventing HIV infection in women.
sections.limitations: The blinded phase was stopped early, which limited blinded safety data over 24 months. In one of the four infections in the cabotegravir group, retrospective testing showed HIV was already present at enrollment, and detection of HIV infection was delayed in several participants, highlighting how hard conventional HIV testing is with potent long-acting PrEP. Viral load testing to catch infections early may be a barrier to rollout in low- and middle-income settings.
sections.practice_impact: Together with HPTN 083, HPTN 084 established long-acting injectable cabotegravir as a PrEP option that does not depend on a daily pill, and it was the first trial to show an injectable superior to oral PrEP in women. It shifted prevention programs toward offering choice, especially for people for whom daily pills are hard to take or to hide.

In a random subset of 405 TDF-FTC participants, 812 (42.1%) of 1929 plasma samples had tenofovir concentrations consistent with daily use.
Although both products for HIV prevention were generally safe, well tolerated, and effective, cabotegravir was superior to TDF-FTC in preventing HIV infection in women.
